title: Analytic Spread Complexity from Level Statistics: From Chaos to Integrability
authors: Pallab Basu, Suman das, Bigboy Madlala
abstract: Spread complexity has emerged as a useful probe of quantum chaos, yet the microscopic spectral origin of its characteristic finite-time peak remains incompletely understood. We develop an analytic framework that relates spread complexity directly to local spectral statistics. Starting from an energy-space representation of the Krylov kernel, we show that the kernel is approximately banded, leading to a rapidly convergent diagonal expansion dominated by nearby levels in the ordered spectrum. Motivated by this structure, we propose an approximate kernel-universality hypothesis: after unfolding, the Krylov kernel is well approximated by that of a uniform lattice. Combining this universal kernel with local spectral statistics yields a simple analytic expression for spread complexity in terms of the Fourier transforms of the $k$-th nearest-neighbour spacing distributions. In particular, at leading order, the finite-time peak is controlled by the Fourier transform of the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution. The resulting framework describes both chaotic random-matrix ensembles and the integrable Poisson limit, identifies the spectral origin of the complexity peak and its late-time behaviour, and provides a direct connection between Krylov dynamics and spectral statistics.
summary: This theoretical work develops an analytic framework to understand 'spread complexity,' a measure used to probe quantum chaos. By analyzing the structure of the Krylov kernel in energy space, the authors derive a formula linking this complexity directly to the Fourier transforms of nearest-neighbor level spacing distributions. This successfully explains the spectral origin of the characteristic peak observed in chaotic systems while correctly predicting the monotonic behavior in integrable limits.
main_problem: The paper aims to resolve the microscopic spectral origin of the characteristic finite-time peak observed in 'spread complexity,' a key diagnostic tool for quantum chaos.
main_result: It derives an analytic expression for spread complexity based on local spectral statistics, successfully describing both chaotic random-matrix ensembles and the integrable Poisson limit. This framework directly connects Krylov dynamics to spectral properties.
method: The authors develop an analytic framework by analyzing the energy-space representation of the Krylov kernel, exploiting its approximate banded structure to relate complexity to Fourier transforms of nearest-neighbor spacing distributions.
model_or_system: The analysis concerns time evolution governed by a time-independent Hermitian Hamiltonian H on a quantum many-body system. The core mathematical tool is the Krylov kernel derived from this energy spectrum.
key_observables: Spread complexity, $C(t)$; finite-time peak structure; local spectral statistics (nearest-neighbor spacing distributions).
important_parameters: The analysis considers regimes ranging from chaotic random-matrix ensembles to the integrable Poisson limit. The large-$D$ limit is frequently employed.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include the approximate banded nature of the Krylov kernel and utilizing an 'approximate kernel-universality hypothesis' relating it to a uniform lattice.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of complexity approximations using successive diagonals of the kernel, comparing exact results against truncated series expansions for both chaotic and Poisson regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the energy-space representation of spread complexity; it then uses the banded structure to derive a master formula linking complexity to spectral statistics; finally, it applies this framework to analyze known limits (chaotic vs. integrable) to pinpoint the origin of the peak.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between dynamical measures like complexity and fundamental spectral statistics provides deep insight into quantum chaos, which is relevant for understanding energy level spacing in complex quantum systems studied in AMO physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Comparison of the exact spread complexity C(t) with the successive approx- imations C(0)(t) = C0, C(1)(t), C(2)(t), and C(3)(t). The left panel shows the full time evolution, while the right panel provides an enlarged view of the region around the max- imum; the vertical dashed lines indicate the corresponding peak positions. The figure demonstrates that the exact complexity is accurately reproduced by retaining only the first few diagonals of the Krylov kernel.

Figure 2. Heat map of the Krylov kernel K(i, j). The colour scale represents log10(⟨|K(i, j)|⟩), where the ensemble average is taken over 50 realizations. The logarith- mic scale is used to enhance the visibility of the off-diagonal structure. The figure clearly illustrates the approximately banded nature of the kernel, with the magnitude of its matrix elements decreasing as one moves away from the principal diagonal. Although an ensemble average is shown here, the same qualitative behaviour is observed for individual realiza- tions.

Figure 3. Left: the integrated off-diagonal weight |Wk|, eq. (3.1), versus k on a log–log scale, showing an approximate 1/k2 decay and confirming the banded structure of the kernel. Right: the disorder-averaged participation ratio PR versus D.
